subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the circumcentre of the triangle whose sides are x+y+2=0, 5x−y−2=0, x−2y+5=0.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say what has to be found first when the SIDES are given, and how many vertices you need.
formula_note: After solving the three sides in pairs for the vertices, the circumcentre formula is still SA = SB = SC, equal distance from each vertex. Do not reach for the perpendicular-slope condition here — that method finds the orthocentre, a different triangle centre defined by the altitudes, not by distance.

steps.margin_note: Two marks. Sides are given, so all three vertices must be found first — each vertex is where two of the three lines meet, so there are three pairs to solve.
steps.memory_tip: Three sides means three PAIRS to solve before any distance work can start.

steps.why: The orthocentre needs only two vertices, because two altitudes already fix it, but the equal-distance method compares all three — so all three corners are needed before any distance is written.
common_mistakes: Solving the same pair twice and getting a repeated point.

steps.label: Draw the triangle
steps.margin_note: Worth no mark but worth drawing. The dashed lines are perpendicular BISECTORS — they cut each side in half at a right angle, which is what the equal-distance condition means geometrically.
steps.memory_tip: Perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre.

recall.must_convey: That a triangle is sketched with two perpendicular bisectors meeting at S. Naming the drawing is full credit — it cannot be spoken.

steps.why: The circumcentre is equally far from all three vertices, and the set of points equally far from two vertices IS the perpendicular bisector of the side joining them.
common_mistakes: Drawing altitudes, which give the orthocentre instead.
Drawing medians, which give the centroid.

steps.memory_tip: Square SA = SB; the x² and y² terms cancel and the equation of a straight line is left.

insider_note: The vertices have to be found first — that is two marks before the circumcentre work even begins. Both equations that follow carry a common factor, so divide it out before solving the pair.
